title: The Answer Was on Top
pace_basis: same runtime-anchored pace paragraph as 2026-09-19 and 09-23 (1.907 wps measured)
note: Numbers and acronyms written phonetically for the synth; on screen they render as numerals. Every factual line carries a claim id.

lines.text: A Kodiak woman asked Google when snipe season opens.
Its A I answer said September first.
So on September fifth she shot three snipe.
lines.display: So on September 5th she shot three snipe.

lines.text: At home she looked up the state regulations and saw her mistake. She called troopers and turned herself in.
The trooper's report says the general season opened October eighth.
lines.display: The trooper's report says the general season opened October 8th.

lines.text: So two pages disagreed. Which one can a hunter trust?
That trooper ran her exact search. He got the same wrong answer.
She still pleaded no contest and paid a hundred fifty dollars.
lines.display: She still pleaded no contest and paid $150.

lines.text: She told the Alaska Beacon, I feel terrible.
State spokesman Austin McDaniel thinks it's the first time A I has been cited. He expects more.
lines.display: State spokesman Austin McDaniel thinks it's the first time AI has been cited. He expects more.

lines.text: Weren't there warnings? There were.
Google's help page says A I answers may include mistakes, and to check more than one place.
lines.display: Google's help page says AI answers may include mistakes, and to check more than one place.

lines.text: Google didn't respond to the Beacon's request for comment.
McDaniel says the one source of truth is Fish and Game's regulations and emergency orders.
But that source has a catch.
Fish and Game's own page says its online regulations are simplified, and emergency orders can override them.
So even the official page is a summary.
The answer was on top. What counts sits underneath.
Check the regulations and any emergency order. Fish and Game will mail you a copy.
Before you hunt, what do you check?
